title: Innovation power is concentrating in cross-border urban clusters where patents, science, venture capital, and industrial capability reinforce one another
source_unit: WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026, Ranking of the World's Top 100 Innovation Clusters and cluster methodology
geography: Approximately 140 economies and the world's top 100 sub-national innovation clusters, defined by inventor, scientific-author, and venture-capital geographies

denominator.unit: top innovation clusters ranked by WIPO

patent_metric.value: inventor locations in published patent applications filed through the WIPO Patent Cooperation Treaty

science_metric.value: author affiliations in scientific publications indexed in the Web of Science SCIE

venture_metric.value: locations of companies receiving venture-capital funding

observations.method: WIPO identifies clusters bottom-up without requiring administrative or political boundaries, combining PCT patent applications, scientific publications, and venture-capital activity.
observations.uncertainty: The three metrics measure visible innovation activity and finance, not all innovation, informal knowledge, social value, diffusion, or the distribution of gains within a cluster.
observations.subgroup: Universities, researchers, inventors, startups, venture investors, R&D firms, skilled workers, city-regions, and communities affected by innovation-led growth.
observations.counterinterpretation: A high-density cluster can generate spillovers and new products while also intensifying housing costs, labor competition, exclusion, and dependence on a narrow set of firms or technologies.

observations.period: 2026 ranking; global innovation-intensive clusters normalized by population

denominator.unit: top clusters ranked by innovation intensity

top_five.value: San Jose–San Francisco, Cambridge, Ningde, Boston–Cambridge, and Oxford

observations.method: WIPO combines each cluster's global share of patents, scientific publications, and venture-capital deals and normalizes by estimated cluster population.
observations.uncertainty: Rankings are sensitive to geocoding, population estimates, fractional counting, metric coverage, and the choice to measure intensity rather than absolute scale.
observations.subgroup: Residents of innovation-intensive city-regions, technology workers, research institutions, firms, local governments, and populations exposed to cluster spillovers or displacement.
observations.counterinterpretation: Per-capita intensity favors smaller high-density clusters and does not mean they have the largest absolute economic, employment, or geopolitical impact.

observations.period: 2026; national and regional distribution of top innovation-intensive clusters

united_states.unit: top-ten intensity clusters located in the United States

united_kingdom.unit: top-ten intensity clusters located in the United Kingdom

other_leaders.value: one each in China, Finland, the Netherlands, and the Republic of Korea
other_leaders.unit: reported country distribution among the top ten

battery_energy_signal.value: Ningde and Daejeon add visible battery and energy-technology weight to the intensity leaders

observations.method: WIPO aggregates cluster-level patent, science, and venture-capital activity and reports the country distribution and technology composition of the top ten intensity ranking.
observations.uncertainty: Country labels describe cluster location, not national ownership or complete value-chain control; cross-border firms, workers, suppliers, and capital can connect multiple jurisdictions.
observations.subgroup: National innovation systems, city-regions, industrial firms, research universities, energy and battery workers, investors, and policymakers seeking technological sovereignty.
observations.counterinterpretation: Concentration can coexist with broad global diffusion of technologies and with innovation activity outside the top-ten intensity clusters.

observations.period: 2021-2025; scale of source data used for the 2026 cluster methodology

pct_applications.unit: PCT patent applications published between 2021 and 2025, approximately

inventor_addresses.unit: inventor addresses in the PCT dataset, approximately

cluster_boundary.value: clusters can span several municipalities, sub-federal states, or more than one country

observations.method: The WIPO methodology geocodes inventor and scientific-author locations, matches them to cluster polygons, incorporates population estimates, and uses fractional counting for people associated with multiple locations.
observations.uncertainty: Geocoding and fractional counting improve comparability but cannot fully capture remote work, institutional collaboration, hidden innovation, or the direction of causal spillovers.
observations.subgroup: Mobile researchers, inventors, firms, universities, cross-border regions, venture-backed companies, and local communities inside or outside cluster boundaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: A cross-border cluster definition can reveal real economic linkages while obscuring the public institutions, labor systems, and communities that bear uneven costs and benefits.

related_sources.claim: WIPO 2026 cluster-ranking landing page and ranking scope.
WIPO Global Innovation Index series and 2026 release context.

boundary: This record adds a place-based innovation-power route linking patents, scientific production, venture capital, urban concentration, industrial capability, technological sovereignty, and uneven local consequences. It is an index and geospatial methodology, not a complete innovation census, causal regional-growth estimate, firm-level ownership history, respondent-level experience, or proof that cluster activity produces broad-based welfare.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official WIPO GII 2026 cluster-ranking pages and methodology were reviewed for the three metrics, top-intensity cluster ranks, country distribution, battery and energy signal, PCT application and inventor-address counts, population normalization, and cross-border cluster rule.
